lesson.title: Forming Participles
lesson.subtitle: -ar → -ado (hablado), -er/-ir → -ido (comido, vivido), plus irregulars hecho (fact) and visto (vista)

hook.title: Regular -ado / -ido and the Two Cognate Irregulars: Hecho & Visto
hook.content: Almost every verb in Spanish forms its participle regularly: -ar → -ado, -er/-ir → -ido. And what about the two most common irregulars: hacer ('to do/make') → hecho ('done/made') and ver ('to see') → visto ('seen')? You already know both from English! Visto is the exact word in 'Hasta la vista' and 'vista/vision'. And hecho comes from Latin factum ('fact/feat') with BOTH Spanish sound shifts firing at once: initial f- → silent h-, and medial -ct- → -ch-!

pattern.title: Double Duty: El Hecho = 'The Fact'
pattern.content: Just like English 'fact' comes from Latin 'thing done', Spanish el hecho means both 'done/made' (Lo he hecho 'I have done it') and the noun 'the fact' (de hecho = 'in fact / actually')!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: hablado, comido, hecho, visto, lo he hecho, lo he visto
exercises.meaning: spoken (hablar → -ado), eaten (comer → -ido), done / made (hacer → factum), seen (ver → vista), I have done it, I have seen it

exercises.prompt: Spanish 'el hecho' ('that which is done', from Latin 'factum' via f-→h- and -ct-→-ch-) is the exact twin of which four-letter English noun meaning 'a proven truth'?
exercises.meaning: a fact (Latin factum) is literally 'a thing done' (hecho)!
exercises.explanation: Latin facere ('to do/make') → participle factum → English fact/feat and Spanish hecho.

exercises.prompt: Convert 'confirmar' into its past participle ('confirmed') by swapping -ar for -ado:

exercises.idea: ask a friend if they have seen the movie/house: 'Have you seen the house?'
exercises.explanation: ¿Has visto la casa? — visto stays invariable (-o) even though la casa is feminine!

diagnosis.cue: After haber (he/has/ha/hemos), the participle NEVER changes for gender: ¿Has visto la casa?

summary.outcome: Form regular -ado/-ido participles and deploy hecho (hacer) and visto (ver) after haber.

use_example.german: Lo he hecho hoy y ya he visto la casa.
use_example.english: I have done it today and I have already seen the house.

summary.takeaway: hecho = Latin factum (f→h, ct→ch); visto = vista — and participles after haber never change ending.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([1702] The haber Auxiliary): drill he, has, ha, hemos across life experiences and today's actions.

hablado.etymology_derivation: Past participles after haber NEVER change for gender or number — always end in -o!

hecho.english_meaning: done, made (participle of hacer); fact (el hecho)
hecho.shift_rule: Double sound shift: factum → hecho (f→h AND ct→ch!)
hecho.etymology_derivation: Look at Latin factum → Spanish hecho: initial f- became silent h-, AND medial -ct- became -ch-!

visto.etymology_derivation: You already know it from 'Hasta la vista'!

he.etymology_derivation: Latin habēre split into tener (possession: tengo un coche) and haber (auxiliary: he hablado, plus hay)!

has.etymology_derivation: Never separate haber from its participle!

hacer.context_translation: I want to make a reservation.
hacer.etymology_derivation: Latin facere shifted initial f- to silent h- in Spanish: hacer. English keeps the f in fact and factory.

ver.context_translation: I am going to see it/him today.
ver.etymology_derivation: Pronouns can hook directly onto the tail of the infinitive: verlo ('to see it/him')!

vivir.etymology_derivation: Latin vīvere — English vivid, revive, survive.

confirmar.etymology_derivation: confirmación → confirmar. Strip -ación, attach -ar. One rule turns hundreds of nouns into verbs.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.
